Approval Page One — Vendor Onboarding

This fixture is the markdown form of the T8 spike fixture (scripts/pdf-spike/fixtures/approval.html), carrying the same structural tokens so scripts/zs/pdf-validate.sh — the validator contract named in the T8 ticket — validates a T9 export unchanged: three headings, a data table whose every row carries a distinct token, a code block with a marker line, and enough running text to span three printed pages at US Letter with 0.75in margins.

Unlike the spike fixture it carries no remote image. A PDF export must not reach the network, so the exported document's content-security policy denies every remote subresource and the browser is launched with DNS resolution disabled. A document that does reference a remote image renders a visible placeholder rather than fetching it.

Filler paragraph 1. The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the riverbank while the autumn light fades across the workshop floor. Every vendor approval cycle begins with a short intake form, a signature block, and a checklist of the materials the studio expects back before the piece moves into production scheduling.

Filler paragraph 2. Reviewers read the brief twice: once for the stone specification and once for the metal alloy and plating notes. A third pass checks the delivery window against the studio's current backlog, since late vendor turnaround is the single largest cause of missed launch dates across the last four collections.

Filler paragraph 3. The approval record itself is short, but the context around it is not: photography references, prior revision notes, and a running thread of email correspondence all attach to the same record so that anyone opening it six months later can reconstruct why a decision was made and who made it.

Filler paragraph 4. Links are kept as links in a document export, so the vendor handbook and any attachment shared alongside this document stay reachable from the printed page instead of being flattened into unlabelled text.

Filler paragraph 5. Each row of the materials table above carries its own distinct value in the last column, so an automated text-extraction pass can confirm every individual row survived rendering rather than the whole table having been flattened into a single image during export. The exact per-row values are defined once, in the table itself, and are not restated here.

Filler paragraph 6. Between the table and the code block sits the section of the brief that explains how the approval id is generated: a short deterministic function keyed off the vendor code, the collection season, and a monotonic counter, so that two approvals issued the same day never collide even when generated by different reviewers working offline.

Approval ID Generator

def approval_id(vendor_code: str, season: str, counter: int) -> str:
    # PDF_SPIKE_CODE_MARKER_7f3a
    return f"{vendor_code.upper()}-{season}-{counter:04d}"

Filler paragraph 7. The comment on the second line of the code block above is the line an automated extraction check looks for. Its exact text is defined once, inside the code block itself, and is deliberately not repeated anywhere else in this document, so finding it in extracted text is proof the code block rendered rather than proof the phrase merely occurs somewhere.

Filler paragraph 8. Code is never collapsed in a document export. The viewer caps how much it will syntax-highlight and how tall a code block may grow on screen; the printed document has neither cap, so a long block wraps and flows across pages instead of being clipped at a scroll boundary the reader cannot reach on paper.

Filler paragraph 9. Vendor relationships at this scale are managed through a small number of long-running threads rather than one-off tickets, and the approval record is the anchor every later message in that thread refers back to, which is why its rendering fidelity — headings, tables, code, and links all surviving a headless export — is worth binding to a fixture rather than checking by eye.

Filler paragraph 10. This paragraph, and the ones immediately following, exist purely as layout ballast: measured filler whose length was tuned against this exact print stylesheet so the fixture lands on three pages, not two and not four, when exported through the route the T8 memo picked.

Filler paragraph 11. Ballast continues. The workshop's Tuesday intake window closes at noon; anything arriving after that rolls to the following week's queue automatically, and the queue position is recorded on the approval record itself so a vendor can see where they stand without opening a separate ticket.

Filler paragraph 12. Ballast continues. Historically, the studio found that approval pages reviewed on a phone screen were approved 30% faster than the same page reviewed on a laptop, which is a minor detail but one reason the print layout is kept deliberately narrow and linear rather than using a multi-column layout that would need horizontal scrolling on a small screen.

Filler paragraph 13. Ballast continues. Blockquotes, lists and rules all come through the same document-mode component map:

A quoted line from the vendor brief, kept as a blockquote so the printed document shows the same structure the viewer does.

  • First checklist item, kept as a list rather than a run of paragraphs.
  • Second checklist item, with inline code that stays monospaced.
  • Third checklist item.

Filler paragraph 14. Ballast continues. The last paragraph restates the point of the whole fixture: it is not a real vendor document, it is a stand-in shaped like one, built so the export check rests on a fixed, hashed input rather than on an ad hoc test page assembled differently for each run.

Filler paragraph 15. Ballast continues, and ends here. The three headings, four table row tokens and one code marker line above are the only things the validator asserts on; everything else on these pages is length, tuned so the page count itself is a check worth making.
